en: The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai explains the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*) as follows: the three kinds of wisdom (*san-zhi*) are called "contemplation" (*guan*); the three truths (*san-di*) are called "the world" (*shi*);

the three contemplations (*san-guan*) are the "words" (*yu*); and the fundamental source is the "sound" (*yin*). Regarding "Attaining Great Power" (*Dashi*), the *Siyi jing* states: "When I set foot..."
Because his dwelling causes the three-thousandfold world system and the palaces of Māra to tremble, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka* states:
"May my world be no different from that of Avalokiteśvara and the others."
The Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
“Because you vowed to take up the great trichiliocosm, I shall now name you Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) serve as the feet; by planting them in the ground of the Three Truths, one moves the ten dharma-realms, such that all places where views and attachments reside are entirely shaken and overturned, and so forth.
Regarding "without rest," the *Suyāma-sūtra* states:

"If a single day and night were as long as the kalpas of the sands of the Ganges River, thirty such days would constitute a month, and twelve such months a year; after passing through hundreds of thousands of billions of billions of kalpas, one might encounter a single Buddha."

Having thus encountered Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, practicing all forms of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and cultivating meritorious virtues, he subsequently received his prediction; because his mind never ceases its activity, it is called "Unceasing" (*Aksobhya*).

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: one contemplates emptiness without dwelling in emptiness, emerges into the conventional without dwelling in the conventional, and enters the middle way without dwelling in the middle; to simultaneously illumine both truths is called "unresting."
Regarding "Treasure Hand" (*Ratnapāṇi*), the *Samantaprasādika* states:

"Clad in the armor of supreme virtue, such that even a Buddha cannot thwart or defeat him; he causes the Mahāyāna to be explained, and even in his dreams does not set his mind upon the Two Vehicles. Constantly using a sincere heart and a heart of various supernormal wisdoms to preach and proclaim for others, he has no greed or attachment toward precious treasures; therefore, he is named Treasure Hand."

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the inconceivable three truths are called the "jewels," and the threefold contemplation within a single mind is called the "palm. Because one grasps these jewels of truth by means of this palm of contemplation for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others, it is called the "Jewel Palm" (Ratnapāṇi).
Regarding the term "Bhaiṣajyarāja" (Medicine King), the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"I vow that when each of the one thousand four Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa first attains enlightenment, I shall make offerings to them all; when these Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa, I shall erect stupas for them all; throughout the eon’s end and its afflictions, I shall rescue and protect all beings; and amidst the calamities of war and pestilence, I shall act as a great king of physicians, and only thereafter shall I become a Buddha."
The Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
"I shall now name you Fire-Purifying Medicine King; in the future you will become a Buddha, namely the Tathāgata Lohita.
Regarding this, the *Guānxīn* (Contemplation of the Mind) commentary states: [and so forth].
The following section lacks the commentary on the seven bodhisattvas.
Regarding "Bhadrapāla," this means "Good Protector" (Śubharakṣita) and is also called "Worthy Protector.
The *Sañcayagāthā* (*Siyi jing*) states:
"If sentient beings hear his name, they will certainly attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, he is named 'Well-Protected' (*Sugupta*).
Regarding the contemplative interpretation: the correct contemplation of the Middle Way is the foremost among all virtues; therefore, it is called "Well-Protected."
“Maitreya” means “The Kindly One” (Cishi) in this language.
The *Suyāma-sūtra* states:
“If sentient beings see him, they immediately attain the samādhi of the compassionate mind; therefore, he is named Maitreya.”
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
"When the king saw the elephant trainer taming the elephant, a mind of loving-kindness arose within him; from this, he received the name Maitreya.
The *Sūtra of the Flower of Compassion* states:
"He made a vow to protect sentient beings amidst the kalpas of swords and fire.

Now, observing the interpretation, the Middle Way’s correct contemplation is precisely unconditional great compassion (*anālambana-mahāmaitrī*). By the power of the roots of goodness of this compassion, all mental factors (*caitta*) enter into the dharma of great compassion of the same essence (*sābhāva-mahāmaitrī*), thereby departing from all that is unwholesome; thus he is called Maitreya.
It is further said that "Maitreya" is his family name, and "Ajita" is his given name; this translates as "Unconquerable," as explained in detail in the subsequent text.
The commentary on "Ratnakūṭa" is missing from below.
Regarding the term "Guide" (Śāstṛ), the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* states:

"Because he gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings who have fallen onto deviant paths and leads them to enter the right path, without seeking any reward for his kindness, he is called a 'Guide' (Nāyaka).

Regarding the contemplative interpretation: the wondrous wisdom of the three contemplations guides all practices so that they do not fall into the two extremes, but rather all enter into right contemplation; therefore, it is called a 'Guide'."
Regarding those points not yet explained, they shall await subsequent annotations, and so forth.
Sixth, the section beginning with "Thus" (evam) is the concluding sentence.
Third, as for the listing of the miscellaneous assembly: while it was formerly called the assembly of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), there are actually noble ones (ārya) among them.
The old translation "the assembly of worldly beings" (súzhòng) implies that there are those who have attained the Way among them;
the old translation "the assembly of devas and humans" (tiānrén zhòng) implies that there are dragons and ghosts among them;
neither is appropriate.

Now, they are called the "miscellaneous assembly" because their scope is comprehensive; that which is referred to as the five destinies, the two realms, and the eight classes is why they are termed "miscellaneous.

Even the Vaipulya sutras list the hells, and the *Antarābhava Sūtra* also transforms beings in the formless realm; these all appear according to the capacities of sentient beings and cannot be treated as uniform parallels, nor can their sequence be fixed.

The old tradition holds that the host should yield the way to guests; however, the *Anantamukha-sādhaka-nirdeśa Sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing) shares the same principle as this sutra, clarifying that kings, ministers, scholars, and ladies of the realm sit together on the same mat, regardless of whether they are host or guest yielding to one another.
The transmitters of the sūtra have arranged these [beings] in their textual order; however, there may be a specific underlying intention that has not yet been fully clarified.

Observing this passage now, it consists of eight sections: first, Śakra is designated; next, the Four Kings are listed; dragons precede birds; and spirits and deities appear twice. For these reasons, they are called the "miscellaneous assembly," and one cannot speak of them as following a fixed sequential order.

Furthermore, regarding the "mixed assembly," within this group there are those who have attained the Way and those who have not; they are called "mixed" because their karmic retributions and their physical appearances and attire are mixed.
Among them, those who have attained the Way of the Two Vehicles are called "mixed" because their untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is mixed with ignorance and afflictions (*kleśa*).
Among them, those who have attained the Way of the Bodhisattvas are called "mixed" because their skillful means (*upāya*) are mixed with the various capacities of sentient beings.
Among those who attain the Way of the Buddha, a single dharma encompasses all dharmas; therefore, it is called "mixed. Such is the meaning of "mixed":
how could it be judged by the physical forms of ordinary people, nor could it be judged by the five classes of beings, humans, devas, and so forth? For this reason, it is called "mixed."
This is an explanation according to the teachings, and so forth.
Regarding "Śakra Devānām Indra": *Indra* is also called *Candra*; this translates as "The Able One," who acts as the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Trāyastriṃśa is translated here as "Thirty-three. There are eight cities on each of the four sides; together with the city of Sudarśana, they total thirty-three, all situated atop Mount Sumeru.

Sumeru is translated here as "Peaceful Brilliance" (Anming) and is composed of the four precious substances. It is three million three hundred and sixty thousand li in height and breadth. As this is the sovereign of the heavens of desire, it is listed first.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 40, states:
"A certain bhikṣu asked the Buddha:
'For what reason is he named Śakra Devānām Indra?'"
He replied:
"In his former life as a human, he practiced sudden giving and was capable of acting as a leader;
therefore, he is named Śakra Devānām Indra. Why is he named Puraṃdara?"
“Because when he was a human being, he practiced giving repeatedly.
“Why is he named Maghavā?
“Because that was his name when he was originally a human being.”
"Why is he named Sāmbhava?
"Because when he was formerly a human being, he gave this robe as a gift.
"Why is he named Kauśika?"
"It was because of his original clan name when he was a human.
"Why is he named Śacīpati? "Śacī is the wife and Pati is the husband."
"Why is he named 'Thousand Eyes'?

"In his former life as a human, he was intelligent; once, while sitting in contemplation, he considered a thousand kinds of meanings, observing and weighing them. Therefore, he is named 'Thousand Eyes.'"
"Why is he named Indri?
Because he is the lord of thirty-two heavens.
The *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng), fascicle three, states:
"The name of the Heavenly Lord is Kauśika.

Regarding the teaching gate: in the *Āgamas*, Śakra is an Anāgāmin; in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he is clarified as being from the ten directions. Those who pose difficult questions regarding Prajñā are all named Śakradevendra.

Furthermore, within the *Bieyuan* (Separate and Perfect), it is clearly explained that Śakra-devānām-indra attained the Śūraṅgama-samādhi; his internal realization was distinct [from others], and after two thousand twenty-four kalpas beyond the Bhadrakalpa, he will become a Buddha named the World-Honored One Without Attachment (*Vigata-āsanga*), and so forth.

Regarding the "Original and the Traces": the ten abodes, the practices, and the stages of approach constitute thirty; the ten grounds constitute one; equal enlightenment constitutes two; and wondrous enlightenment is the principal. Together they dwell in the heaven of the primary meaning and partake of the nectar of the true aspect—this is the "Original. To reside upon the summit of Mount Sumeru is the "Trace."

Regarding the interpretation of contemplating the mind for liberation: practicing the ten wholesome deeds oneself and encouraging others to rejoice in them—these thirty wholesome deeds are all empty, all provisional, and all the Middle Way; this constitutes the thirty-three gates of contemplation.

The three devaputras, beginning with "Named Moon" (Candranāman), are like internal ministers such as high officials or prime ministers; some say they are simply the devaputras of the Three Luminaries.
"Named Moon" is the devaputra Candrasiri, who should be visualized as Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
"Universal Fragrance" (Samantagandha) is the devaputra Tisya, who should be visualized as Gaganagañja.
Ratnaprabha (Precious Light) is the Devaputra Ratnamati-sūrya (Jewel-Mind Sun), who is manifested as Avalokiteśvara.
This is the explanation in terms of the fundamental and the trace.

Regarding the contemplative interpretation: the three contemplations are the two wisdoms, and the three wisdoms are the three lights. The three wisdoms arise from the three truths; the truths are the "Heaven" (deva) and the wisdoms are the "Sons" (putra), and so forth.

The "Four Great Heavenly Kings" are the external ministers of Śakra, like military generals; they dwell upon four mountains made of precious jewels, which are half the height of Sumeru and twenty-four thousand li in breadth.
In the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, here translated as "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó) or "Peace for the People" (Ànmín). He dwells on the Golden Mountain and presides over two classes of spirits:
the Gandharvas and the Piśācas.
To the south is Virūḍhaka, which is translated here as "Increasing" or "Deliverance"; he dwells on Mount Vaiḍūrya and presides over two classes of spirits:
the Pretas and the Kumbhāṇḍas.

Vaiśravaṇa of the West—here translated as "Non-Excellent Retribution," also called "Evil Eye," and also called "Diverse Speech"—resides on the White Silver Mountain and commands two classes of spirits:
the venomous nāgas and the piśācas.
The northern Vaiśravaṇa is here called Citraśrava (Various Hearings) or Bahuśruta (Much-Hearing). He dwells on Mount Sphaṭika (Crystal Mountain) and commands two classes of spirits:
rākṣasas and yakṣas.
Each leads two spirits and does not allow them to afflict people; therefore, they are called the World Protectors (*Lokapāla*). Regarding their fundamental and manifested aspects:

fundamentally, the four kings—Eternity, Bliss, Self, and Purity—protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma so that outsiders cannot take its branches and leaves to cut it down or destroy it. King Eternity protects the twin trees of Eternity and Impermanence in the East; King Bliss protects the twin trees of Bliss and Non-bliss in the South; King Self protects the twin trees of Self and Non-self in the West; and King Purity protects the twin trees of Purity and Impurity in the North.

The branches and trunk are a metaphor for permanence; the flowers, for selfhood; the fruit, for bliss; and the lush leaves, for purity. Because one protects these flowers and fruits, constantly benefiting all sentient beings, one manifests as a Caturmahārāja to protect the world.

Regarding the interpretation through contemplation (*guanjie*): the wisdom that contemplates the Four Truths is itself the Four Kings; by eliminating the two delusions of craving and views under each truth, one protects against the eight types of craving and views.

Above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is the Yama Heaven; this is translated as "Good Time" (*śubhakāla*), while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls it "Exquisite Goodness. It is located three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Above the Heaven of Good Fortune (Sutāra) is Tuṣita, which is translated as "Wondrous Foot" (Miaozu). It is as far from the Yama Heaven as the earth is [from it], yet it is not listed here; this is merely an abbreviation. Why is this so?

The gods of the lower heavens are dull-witted, while those of the higher heavens are attached to pleasure; yet even they know to assemble here, let alone those who are neither attached nor dull—how could they not come?

"Īśvara" refers to the fifth [heaven], and "Maheśvara" refers to the sixth; these are the heavens where one creates the five desires for oneself (*svayam-nirmita-kāma*) and where others create the five desires for one (*para-nirmita-kāma*), and so forth.
Some say that this refers to Maheśvara at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This [position] should not be taken as transcending to that [level].
Regarding the "original" and the "traces": these two heavens are originally abiding in the concentrations of *Īśvara* and *Īśvararāja*, while their "traces" manifest merely as those two heavens.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: entering emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the Contemplation of Sovereignty; entering the Middle Way (*madhyama*) is the Contemplation of Great Sovereignty, and so forth.
Next, the heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) are listed.

"Sahā" is translated here as "Endurance" (*kṣānti*); because the sentient beings of that land abide in the ten non-virtues and are unwilling to seek liberation, the land is named after its inhabitants, and is thus called "Endurance."
The *Karunāpuṣpa Sūtra* states:
"Why is it called Sahā?
Because all these sentient beings endure the three poisons and various afflictions, it is therefore named the Land of Endurance."
It is also called "Mixed," because it is mixed with the nine paths and they dwell together, and so forth.

As for "Brahma" (梵), this is translated as "Free from Desire" (離欲); having eliminated the fetters of the lower realms and ascending to the Form Realm (色界), it is thus named "Free from Desire," and is also termed "Exalted Purity" (高淨).

"Śikhin" is translated here as "Crest" (頂髻). Furthermore, in foreign lands fire is called *jyotiṣ* (樹提), and *śikhin* [is derived from this]; this king originally practiced the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) and destroyed the afflictions of the desire realm, so he was named after that virtue.

However, while the sutra mentions both the Brahma King and Śikhin, which might suggest they are two different individuals, according to the *Śāstra*, Śikhin is correctly identified as the king; thus, it appears that the sutra here refers to a single person by citing his title and name.

Abiding in the intermediate dhyāna, with vitarka and vicāra within and verbal expression without, one who attains mastery becomes a king; practicing dhyāna alone makes one a Brahma-minister, while adding the four immeasurable minds makes one a king.
In the first dhyāna, there are the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā heavens; here, by mentioning the king [Mahābrahmā], all are included.
"Radiance" refers to the second dhyāna, which includes the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara heavens;
the third dhyāna includes the Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna heavens.

In the fourth dhyāna, there is the Guhyaka body which is likewise without obstruction; there is the Immeasurable Guhyaka which also receives blessings; there is the Guhyakaphala which is also the Vast Fruit; and there is the Asaṃjñi-sattva Guhyaka which is also without perception.
Furthermore, there are five types of Anāgāmins:

Avṛha, Atapa, Sudarśana, Sudṛśa, and Akaniṣṭha; as well as Maheśvara, who is Mahāsvara. The scriptural text is abbreviated and does not list them all in full, but they are equal to these various devas.
For example, there are the teachings on the Exoteric and Esoteric (Kyo-mon), the Fundamental and Traces (Hon-jaku), and the Contemplation of the Mind (Kan-shin);

reflect upon these yourself. Next, regarding the listing of the Eight Dragons: "Nanda" means Joy, and "Bhadra" means Good; as brothers, they constantly protect Magadha, causing rain to fall at the proper times so that the country has no years of famine. King Bimbisāra held an assembly once a year, and when the common people heard of it, they all rejoiced; it was from this that they derived their names. These are the ones subdued by Maudgalyāyana, who dwell within the ocean.
Regarding the explanation of the fundamental and the provisional: fundamentally, he dwells on the Stage of Joy; provisionally, he resides among the seas.
Regarding the explanation through contemplation: the three contemplations are themselves the Middle Way, which gives rise to the joy of the Dharma.
"Sāgara" (Sagala) is named after his dwelling in the ocean; as referred to in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the old translations state he was named after his native country.
In essence, he dwells in the great ocean of the Perfection of Wisdom (*Prajñāpāramitā*), while in appearance, he resides in the vast blue sea.
"Vaśavartin" (Andhaka) means "Many Heads" in this language, and is also called "Precious Renown. He dwells within the waters.
Fundamentally, he abides in the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms; as a trace, he manifests with many heads.
"Contemplation" refers to the contemplation that enters into the provisional, which discriminates immeasurable dharma-gates, and so forth.

"Takṣaka" means "Manifesting Poison," also called "Many-Tongued" or "Double-Tongued"; he fundamentally dwells in the dharma-gate of unhindered eloquence in joyful exposition, yet in his manifested trace he appears as one with many tongues.
“Anavatapta” is named after its lake; this is translated as “Without Heat.
Regarding the Lake Anavatapta, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 18, states:

“At the summit of the Snowy Mountains there is a lake called Lake Anavatapta. Within it is a hall supported by five pillars, which takes its name from the lake; the Dragon King constantly dwells therein.”
The dragons of Jambudvīpa have three afflictions:
first, hot winds and hot sands strike their bodies, burning their skin, flesh, and marrow, causing them great suffering;

second, fierce winds suddenly arise and blow away their palaces, causing them to lose their precious ornaments and garments, and their dragon bodies to become exposed, which causes them great suffering.
Third, when the various nāgas are enjoying themselves, the garuḍas enter their palaces, seize the newly born nāga children, and devour them, causing them fear and the torment of distress.
This lake is free from these three afflictions; if a bird conceives the thought of going there, it immediately dies. Therefore, it is named the Lake Without Torment (Anavatapta).
The fundamental abiding is cool, eternal, blissful, self, and pure; its manifested traces dwell in the cool pond.

As for "contemplation," it refers to the wondrous wisdom of the three contemplations, which purifies the vexing swarms of the five abodes and avoids the scorching sands of the two deaths, and so forth.
“Mānasa” is translated here as “Great Body,” or alternatively as “Great Mind” or “Great Power.
When the asuras pushed back the ocean to submerge the city of Sudarśana, this dragon coiled its body to block the seawater.
The Dharma-gate of the Primordial Abiding Boundless Body takes its trace as its great substance.
As for "contemplation," it refers to the Middle Way’s correct contemplation of its nature as vast and extensive, and so forth.
"Utpala" is translated here as "the dark-colored lotus pond"; the dragon dwells therein and is named after that pond.
The fundamental abiding is the Lotus Samādhi, while its provisional manifestation resides in this pond.
As for "contemplation," the three contemplations are the cultivation of causes, and these causes are the lotus flowers.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"The dragons protect the realms for the devas, and when the asuras raise their armies to fight the dragons, it is known that [the dragons] are governed by the devas.

Next are listed the four kinnaras, also called *cintāmaṇi* (or *tandrila*), which here means "doubtful spirits. They resemble humans but have a single horn, and are thus termed "neither human nor non-human" (*manuṣya-amanuṣya*).
The Dharma-pleasure deity of the Heavenly Lord dwells upon the Ten Treasure Mountains; whenever his body manifests extraordinary signs, he immediately performs music above.
When the Buddha preaches the Dharma, the various devas provide stringed songs and play the pañcavīṃśati-tūrya to chant the gates of the Dharma.
The ancients said:

"The Dharma-dhāraṇī recites the Four Noble Truths; the Miao-dhāraṇī recites the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; the Da-dhāraṇī recites the Six Perfections; and the Chi-dhāraṇī recites all three of the preceding."
Now, it is said that he presented the fourfold Dharma-gate.

Abiding in the inconceivable fundamental state, neither arising from nor entering the meditative absorption of cessation, he joined his palms in dhyāna and praised the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses, entrusting his traces to lutes and pipes to sing the praises of the Ten Powers.
Regarding "contemplation": to contemplate that sound and voice are themselves empty, provisional, and the middle, and thus to accord with the three truths, is itself to praise the Buddha.

The four *gandharvas*—here translated as "those who smell fragrance"—take fragrance as their food; they are also called "fragrance-aggregates" (*gandharva-skandha*) because fragrance issues from their bodies. These are the deities of worldly music belonging to the realm of the Heavenly Emperor (*Indra*).

"Entertainment" refers to the performance of acrobatic feats; "the sound of entertainment" refers to drums, cymbals, strings, and wind instruments. "The beautiful" refers to the superior varieties among those acrobatic feats; "beautiful sound" refers to the superior varieties among the strings and wind instruments.

"Āsura" means "without wine" (madya). Flowers were gathered from the four continents and fermented in the great ocean; yet, by the karmic power of the fish and dragons, its flavor remained unchanged. Because they have vowed to sever anger and jealousy, they are called the "Gods Without Wine. They are also called "Not Upright" (abhadra), while Master Tian'an of Mi translated it as "Substantial Integrity" (zhiliang).
"Zhiliang" means straightforwardness and trustworthiness.
This spirit is sycophantic and crooked, and thus its name does not accord with its characteristics.
There are two kinds:
Those categorized as belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) dwell on the shores of the great ocean;
those categorized as belonging to the realm of animals (tiryagyoni) dwell at the bottom of the great ocean.

Regarding "Bāzhi" (Vemacitra), this is translated here as "Bound," or "Bound in Five Places," or "The Five Evils. Because he is bound by objects around his neck such that he cannot escape, he is called "Bound."
It is also said that he is "bound," being bound by Śakra.
His fundamental nature consists of the five fetters used to bind Māra and non-Buddhists; this present image is merely a manifestation of that.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to him as "Supreme Contemplation" (*Parama-darśana*), for by means of the wisdom of the three contemplations, he binds the delusions of the five stages of dwelling and enters into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
*Kharaskandha* means "Broad Shoulders" (廣肩胛) in this language; it is also called "Evil Shadow" (惡陰). Regarding the one who surges the ocean waters, the *Zheng* edition reads "Precious Brocade" (寶錦).

The fundamental abiding consists of the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real; because he compassionately bears the burden of sentient beings, his physical traces manifest as broad shoulders and scapulae.
As for "contemplation," it means that the three contemplations can shake and cover the great ocean of birth and death within the five abodes.

"Vemacitra" means "Pure Mind" (vi-mala-citta) and is also called "Various Doubts" (vicitra-saṃśaya). It is named Vemacitra because it produces sounds from the waters of the ocean; he is the father of Śacī.
The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states:

"A being from the Ābhāsvara Heaven was born upon this earth; the earth caused him to have desire. He entered the sea to wash away his impurity, but fell into the mud and transformed into an egg. After eight thousand years, a girl was born from it, with one thousand heads minus one, and twenty-four hands."

This woman was sporting in the water when a water-essence entered her body; after eight thousand years, she gave birth to a son with twenty-four heads and one fewer than a thousand hands, whose name was Vemacitra, who caused the waves to roar upon the waters of the sea.

Sakra sought out a Gandharva maiden and begot Śacī; by the karmic power of Śakra, he caused her father to dwell in a palace of the seven jewels and took her as his wife. Later, [the father] slandered him, and consequently they engaged in war; [the Asura] trampled the waters of the sea with his feet and attacked Sudarśana with his hands, yet Śakra, through the power of the Prajñā-mantra, could not be harmed.
The *Zheng* edition reads "abiding in seclusion" (*yànjū*).
As for "the fundamental," it refers to the fact that both form and mind are fundamentally pure; this name is derived from its trace-manifestation.
As for "contemplation," it means that the correct contemplation of the Middle Way is itself the pure mind.

“Rāhula” means “Obstructing Holder,” for he is one who obstructs the sun and moon. He is of the animal species, his body is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in length, and his mouth is one thousand *yojanas* wide. His body is adorned with precious jewels. When he gazes upon the celestial maidens and the celestial gardens, if there are people in the four continents who filially support their parents or make offerings to śramaṇas, the various devas exert their power and rain down blades from the sky above;
if they do not do so, the devas enter their palaces and do not emerge.

Furthermore, when the sun emits light that shines directly into one's eyes such that one cannot see, if one raises a palm to block the sun, people of the world all say it is a strange and ominous solar eclipse; they offer various such heterodox explanations.
The same applies when the moon is obscured.
Some produce loud sounds; worldly people say these are the roars of celestial beasts, portending impending chaos and the decline of kings.

They propagate various heterodox doctrines and, fearing the sun, moon, and the seasons, they double the size of their bodies and hiss at the sun and moon with their breath, causing the sun and moon to lose their radiance.
They came to petition the Buddha, who told Rāhu, "Do not swallow the sun and moon.

Rāhu’s limbs trembled and his body broke out in cold sweat; he immediately released the sun and moon. Due to the power of the sun and moon, the power of sentient beings, the power of the Buddha, and the convergence of various causes and conditions, they could not be harmed.
In the past, there was a Brahmin who was wise and practiced extensive giving; he loaded four thousand wagons with food and distributed it in the wilderness.

There was a Buddhist stupa that had been burned by evil people, so he immediately used the water from his four thousand wagons to extinguish the fire and save the stupa. With great joy, he made a vow, wishing to obtain a vast body, the foremost in the realm of desire.
Because he lacked right faith, yet delighted in fighting and war while enjoying giving, he was born in the City of Radiance as Rāhu, the lord of the asuras.
The *Zheng* edition reads "inhaling breath" (*xīqì*).
The original text says, "Contemplation," and so forth.

Next, the four *garuḍas* are listed; this is translated as "Golden Winged" (*jīnshì*). Their wings and feathers are golden in color, and they dwell atop great trees spanning the four continents. The distance between their two wings is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*.
Some say that the *Zhuangzi* calls them *peng*; when the *peng* flies, all other birds follow it with their wings, and it is also called the phoenix (*fènghuáng*).
I maintain that the phoenix does not tread upon living grass, feeds on the kernels of bamboo, and nests in the milky paulownia tree;
as for the golden-winged bird, it devours dragons—how could they be of the same kind?
Regarding "Great Majestic Virtue" (*mahātejas*), its majesty surpasses all its peers, and furthermore, its majesty subdues all dragons. The *Zheng* edition reads "fully endowed."
"Great body" (mahākāya) refers to a great multitude.
"Great fulfillment" (mahāpūrṇa) means that the dragon constantly fulfills his own wishes.
"As one desires" (yatheṣṭa) means that he possesses this jewel on his neck; the *Zheng* edition reads "immovable."

The garuḍa possesses divine power; the male transforms into a son of heaven, and the female changes into a celestial maiden. They transform their dwelling place into a palace of jewels, and there are also foods of a hundred flavors. Yet they must repay their debt by eating dragons: those born from a womb can eat three types of dragons, but cannot eat the fourth; those born from an egg can eat two types, but cannot eat the third; those born from moisture can eat three types, but cannot eat the fourth; and those born through transformation can eat all four.
The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* states: "The correct pronunciation is *garuḍa*.

Each day it devours one dragon king and five hundred small dragons from the eastern mountain; it does the same for the other three directions, beginning again once the cycle is complete, living for eight thousand years."

At the moment of death, losing his strength, he sought to devour the dragon’s son; however, the mother dragon coiled her neck around him so that he could not eat. He immediately became enraged and rushed from Mount Vajra through the ocean, piercing the earth-wheel (pṛthivī-maṇḍala), but he could not pass through the wind-wheel (vāyu-maṇḍala). The wind repelled him, and he surged back up through the original hole to Mount Vajra. This occurred seven times in succession, after which he died upon the mountain peak. His flesh split open and fire erupted, threatening to burn the Jewel Mountain (Ratnaparvata). Nanda rained down rain to extinguish it. His rotten flesh pierced his heart, which struck the wind-wheel again for seven times, falling onto the mountain to become a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi). When a dragon obtains this, he becomes king; even human kings are moved by the power of this jewel.
Next, regarding the individuals listed: "Vaidehī" is her mother; it translates as "Reflection.
"Bimbisāra" is her father; this translates as "Mold-Real."

"Ajātaśatru" means "One Whose Enemy is Not Yet Born. He is also called Vairōcana, which translates as "The Fingerless"; however, his inner attendants protectively call him Sudarśana. "Sudarśana" (Good Vision) is his original name, while "The Fingerless" is a designation based on his physical appearance.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Aja means 'unborn,' and loka means 'enemy.

Because the Buddha-nature is unborn, the enemy of afflictions arises; because the enemy of afflictions arises, one does not see the Buddha-nature. By not giving rise to afflictions, one sees the Buddha-nature."
Furthermore, "Aja" means "unborn," and "Śeṣa" refers to the worldly; because he is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas, he is named Ajātaśatru—this is the original meaning.
The *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* states:

"Ajātaśatru repented before Mañjuśrī and attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti*. At the end of his life, he entered the Piṇḍala hell; upon entering, he immediately emerged, was born in a buddha-field above, and attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. When Maitreya appears, he will return to this realm as the Bodhisattva Acala, and later shall become a Buddha named Viśuddhaviṣaya Tathāgata."
Since its traces are thus, how could its origin be measured?

When the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was preached, he was already among the pure assembly; when the *Nirvāṇa* was reached, he led those who had committed the five grave offenses. How does this differ from Kāśyapa, who received his prediction at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* but was deemed unfit for the entrustment at the *Nirvāṇa*?
One must not become confused by the traces and thereby lose sight of the fundamental source.

Regarding the contemplative understanding: craving is the mother and ignorance is the father; because one harms these, it is called "rebellion," yet rebellion is itself compliance. By proceeding through what is not the Way, one attains penetration into the Buddha-way.
Question:
When the Buddha preached the Dharma among human beings, why was the assembly of people so small?
Answer:
The text is abbreviated and does not record them all, yet those who were present were indeed numerous. The text states:
"Together with various minor kings, wheel-turning sage-kings (*cakravartin-rāja*), and so forth.
In the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (*Wuliangyi jing*), four types of wheel-turning kings are enumerated: the king, the state ministers, the citizens, and the men and women; thus, the assembly was vast.
Question:
Devas, humans, nāgas, and ghosts all see the Buddha and hear the Dharma; why are those in the single realm of hell and the single sphere of the formless not included?
Answer:
This point shall now be elucidated.
Generally, the ascent or descent of the various paths depends on whether one upholds or violates the precepts.

Whether one perceives the Buddha or does not perceive the Buddha depends on whether the vehicle (yāna) is slow or swift. However, because there are coarse and subtle levels of observing the precepts (śīla), the resulting retribution has degrees of excellence or inferiority; and because there are small and great levels of maintaining the vehicle, the perception of the Buddha has provisional or ultimate aspects.

For now, let us briefly judge that the precepts and the vehicle each consist of three grades, and explain this by expanding a single phrase from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* into four propositions; thus, the meaning will become clear: 1. One who observes the precepts but does not maintain the vehicle sees the Buddha provisionally. 2. One who maintains the vehicle but does not observe the precepts sees the Buddha ultimately. 3. One who both observes the precepts and maintains the vehicle sees the Buddha both provisionally and ultimately. 4. One who neither observes the precepts nor maintains the vehicle does not see the Buddha at all. The significance of these points is thus revealed.

First, those who are urgent in both precepts and vehicle; second, those who are lax in precepts but urgent in the vehicle; third, those who are urgent in precepts but lax in the vehicle; fourth, those who are lax in both precepts and vehicle.

If one discusses precepts and the vehicle comprehensively, all wholesome dharmas and all contemplative wisdom may be termed "precepts" and are also all "vehicles. This is the meaning of the five vehicles of humans, devas, and so forth; the precepts of the Path, the Shared, and others are all included within this general sense.

Now, to provide a specific analysis: the three refuges, the five precepts, the ten wholesome paths of action, the eightfold fast, the monastic discipline, and even those factors co-arising with meditative concentration—which are capable of restraining body and speech, preventing the fruits of the evil realms, and securing rebirth among humans and devas—are designated as "precepts" (śīla).

If, upon hearing the sutras, one gives rise to understanding and uses contemplative wisdom to investigate the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and the concepts of arising-and-ceasing versus non-arising-and-non-ceasing; and if this wisdom can destroy afflictions and transport one out of the Triple World, it is called a "vehicle" (yāna).
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Wholesome deeds characterized by signs are immobile and do not emerge; wholesome deeds without signs can move and can emerge.
This is precisely that meaning.

If one is equally urgent in both precepts and vehicle (*śīla-yāna*), then by maintaining lower-grade precepts, one is reborn among humans due to the urgency of the precepts; by maintaining the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) with urgency, one uses a human body to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma during the period of the Tripiṭaka teachings;

by maintaining the Middle Vehicle with urgency, one uses a human retribution-body to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma during the period of the Shared Teachings Mahāyāna and even the various Mahāyāna sūtras that still employ provisional means;

and by maintaining the Supreme Vehicle with urgency, one uses a human retribution-body to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma within the *Avataṃsaka*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and other teachings, as well as within the Perfect teachings—these are precisely those who are listed among the assembly of fellow listeners.

If one maintains the medium grade of precepts with urgency, the retribution will be rebirth among the devas of the desire realm; if one maintains the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) with urgency, then by means of a body among the devas of the desire realm, one will see the Buddha and hear the Dharma during the era of the Tripiṭaka. The rest is as explained above.

If one maintains the superior grade of precepts with urgency and further cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the retribution will be rebirth in the heavens of the Form and Formless Realms; while maintaining the vehicle of the Lesser Vehicle with urgency, one will, by means of a body in the heavens of the Form and Formless Realms, see the Buddha and hear the Dharma within the Tripitaka—the remainder is as explained above.
The first phrase has been explained.

As for those whose precepts are lax but whose vehicle is urgent, their precepts of the three grades are all lax, and thus their retribution is to fall into the three miserable realms; yet, because they hold the Small Vehicle with urgency, they shall see the Buddha and hear the Dharma within the Tripitaka even while possessing bodies in the three miserable realms. The rest is as explained above.
The second phrase has been explained.

As for those whose discipline is urgent while their vehicle is lax: because their threefold discipline is urgent, they receive the bodies of humans and devas in the desire realm, as well as those of the form and formless realms; yet because their three vehicles are lax, even though a Buddha appears in the world and preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, they remain attached to and crave pleasant retributions, indulging in the five desires, neither seeing the Buddha nor hearing the Dharma. This includes the three hundred million households in Śrāvastī, as well as all those who do not see or hear [the teaching], such as the various devas in the three realms who are attached to pleasure.
The explanation of the third phrase is complete.

As for those whose discipline and vehicle are both lax, they will receive retribution in the three miserable realms, neither seeing the Buddha nor hearing the Dharma; the explanation of the fourth phrase is complete.
This text does not list the hells because their precepts are lax, such that the suffering is heavy while the retribution is distant;

those of the Supreme Vehicle are even more lax, being unable to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for other sūtras that do list them, it is because those of the other vehicles are more urgent.

Furthermore, the reason the formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*) are not listed is that because their higher discipline is strict, those born in those heavenly bodies become attached to the flavor of meditative concentration; whereas because the higher vehicle is lax, they are unable to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
As for their inclusion in other sutras, it is simply because in those cases the higher vehicle is strict.

If one attains this understanding, then by examining each of the eight classes of beings, such as devas and nāgas, one will recognize their fundamental conditions and the urgency of their circumstances; thus, the meaning of whether they come or do not come can be fully understood, as explained in detail in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*.

Furthermore, for those who understand the provisional as leading to the real, the meanings of the fundamental and the manifested become increasingly clear; having examined this against one's own contemplative practice, the causality of the three periods of time becomes vividly discernible.
"Each bowed at the Buddha’s feet" summarizes the assembly gathered there.
From "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to the end of the chapter is titled the "Separate Introduction.

The text consists of five parts: first, the assembly gathers; second, the manifestation of auspicious signs; third, the arising of doubt; fourth, the posing of questions; and fifth, the answering of questions.

In the *Guangzhai* [Sutra], the arising of both the favorable and the unfavorable occurs because of the gathering of the assembly; thus, omens appear, and so on until the answering arises from the questioning. Since the answer depends upon the question, and the omen depends upon the gathering of the assembly, this constitutes a reciprocal dependent origination, linked like a chain. Yet, while the introduction to the primary meaning has not yet been fully revealed, even a single explanation based on causes and conditions remains unclear; how much more so when there are two, three, or four conditions, for which there is no discernible direction or purpose?

Now, to clarify the five prefaces: the Preface on the Correct Middle clarifies the One of Principle; the Preface on Assembling the Multitude and Describing People clarifies the One of Person; the Preface on Manifesting Auspicious Omens clarifies the One of Principle; the Preface on Doubtful Thoughts clarifies the One of Practice; and the Preface on Question and Answer clarifies the One of Teaching. This is the explanation by way of causes and conditions (*nidāna*).

Regarding the provisional teaching (*yàojiào*), this introduction introduces the main body; it is neither of the Tripitaka, nor of the Shared, nor of the Distinct, but rather introduces the Perfect and Correct.

Regarding the fundamental and the trace (*běntrì*), if one uses the introduction to introduce the fourfold "oneness" of the original ground within the "Life Span" chapter, this meaning can be understood by itself and need not be recorded here again.
It is said that by contemplating the mind, one may understand [this], and so forth.

Regarding the assembly of the multitude, there are two parts: first, the deportment of the assembled multitude; second, the offerings of the assembled multitude. The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Lotus Sūtra Commentary) identifies this as "abiding in accordance with the Dharma through deportment."
Regarding the term "four assemblies" (catasraḥ parṣadaḥ), the old translation states:
"There are two for the ordained and two for the laity, totaling four assemblies.
This designation is narrow in scope and its meaning is not comprehensive.
Now, based on this single assembly, we further distinguish four types:

the initiating assembly (*janaka-parṣad*), the responsive assembly (*pratipannaka-parṣad*), the influential assembly (*anubhāva-parṣad*), and the assembly for establishing karmic connections (*saṃbandha-parṣad*).

The "initiating" refers to those possessing skillful means, wisdom, and discernment who understand the capacities [of beings] and the timing; they strike, uplift, and stimulate [the assembly] to accomplish beneficial ends. This is like a great elephant knocking down a tree so that its young may be satiated. Specifically, those who initiate the gathering, initiate auspicious signs, and even initiate questions and answers are all termed the initiating assembly.

Those who are "responsive to the occasion" have planted roots of virtue in past lives; when conditions converge and the time ripens—like an abscess ready to burst—they attain the Way upon hearing the teaching without rising from their seats. These are called the assembly responsive to the occasion.

Regarding "shadows and echoes": these are the Buddhas of antiquity and the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas who conceal their perfect supremacy to assist the Dharma King, like the myriad stars surrounding the moon; though they act without effort, their benefit is immense, and this is called the Assembly of Shadows and Echoes.

Regarding those who form a karmic connection (*kemyō*), their power lacks the capacity to guide or stir others, and their virtue does not possess the function of subduing or solemnizing things. Because their past roots were shallow, they are shrouded in outflows and defilements; the three types of wisdom do not arise within them. Although they may see the Buddha and hear the Dharma in the present life, they derive no benefit from the four *siddhāntas*; rather, this serves merely as a causal condition for attaining liberation in the future. These are called the assembly of those who form a karmic connection.
As it is with the assembly of bhikṣus, so it is with the other three assemblies; together they comprise sixteen groups. This is analogous to the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū:

those who preached the Dharma in secret were the "assembled multitude" (*samudita-gaṇa*) of that time; those who heard the Dharma and attained the Way were the "responsive multitude" (*pratibaddha-gaṇa*) of that time; and those who heard the Dharma but were not yet liberated, meeting one another life after life until now—some of whom still abide on the stage of a śrāvaka—were the "multitude for establishing karmic connections" (*pratyaya-gaṇa*) of that time.
In the time of that Buddha, there were likewise four groups of sixteen assemblies; since the Way of this present Buddha is identical, how could he not have them?
These are the sixteen assemblies of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); by analogy, they can also be understood according to the three other teachings.
The provisional and the ultimate (honji-suijaku) can thus be understood.

As for "contemplating the mind," one investigates the object to form contemplation while within the stages of the name-stage and the practice-stage; at that point, one becomes a member of the "karmically connected assembly. Upon entering the stage of semblance, one becomes a member of the "appropriate assembly"; upon entering the stage of partial realization, one becomes a member of the "initiating" or "echoing" assemblies, and so forth.

Regarding "surrounding": when the Buddha first appeared in the world, people did not yet know the Dharma. A being from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven transformed himself into human form, arrived, circumambulated to the right, paid homage, and after paying homage, withdrew to sit and listen to the Dharma.
Because of their reverence for the heavens, people take them as models; this is the explanation based on causes and conditions (*nidāna*).

As for "encircling," it refers to the majestic deportment of circumambulation, symbolizing that the mechanisms of the four gates are activated so that all perceive the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*). When comparing the Perfect against the Partial, there are four corresponding meanings; this is the explanation according to the gate of teaching (*śāsana-mukha*).

Furthermore, as the Buddha’s body is adorned all around with the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana), gazing up at him from the four directions increases the meditative concentration on the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi); this is the understanding through contemplating the mind.
If, by contemplating the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya), one attains the vision of the dharma-body (dharmakāya), this is the understanding through the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku).

Regarding "making offerings" (*pūjā*): generally speaking, all three types of action (*trikarma*) constitute making offerings. To discuss them specifically: being humble, reverent, and performing prostrations is called "respect" (*gaurava*); maintaining focused mindfulness and concentration is called "veneration" (*satkāra*); speaking words that praise and extol is called "eulogy" (*praśaṃsā*); and bestowing material requisites is called "offering" (*pūjā*).
The text here is abbreviated; a full exposition should be understood as it is extensively explained in the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (*Wuliangyi jing*).
Celestial cuisine, celestial incense, celestial bowls, and so forth constitute these offerings.
The Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha and the eighty thousand great beings joined their palms in reverence, gazed up with single-minded devotion in honor, and uttered verses in seven-syllable lines as praise.

Now, regarding the discussion of the assembly of the multitude, as for the reference to that text: in that sutra, after the teaching was concluded, the assembly remained solemnly without dispersing; they continued to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* from their very seats. Thus we know that the offerings of the three karmas must not differ. Using that extensive explanation to clarify this brief one involves no fault in meaning.

From the passage "He preached Mahāyāna sūtras for the sake of all bodhisattvas" down to "he erected a stupa made of the seven treasures with the Buddha's relics," this constitutes the sequence of manifesting signs (*nidāna*).
Master Yao elucidated seven auspicious signs: six manifest in this land, while one is common to other lands;
in both this and those lands, there are six signs each for the manifestation of light and its abiding.

Regarding these six: movement signifies preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, while stillness signifies entering meditative concentration to contemplate the principle; thus, movement and stillness constitute a pair.
The heavens above rain down four kinds of flowers, while the earth below quakes in six ways; these two constitute one pair.
Within the great assembly, joy is harbored, while from without, the Tathāgata radiates light; these two constitute another pair.

Now, it is said that the arising and ceasing [of dharmas] follows the text as Guangzhai did; however, while this makes it easy to grasp the names and meanings, the underlying sense of manifestation and retribution remains unclarified.
Now, we shall establish three pairs: wisdom, concentration, and cause-and-effect-response.
Wisdom refers to the One while explaining the many; concentration concerns the objects of the truths and conditions.
As for the cause, there were the four signs and celestial flowers; as for the fruit, there was the shaking of the earth at six locations.
As for the stimulus, the capacity for the Mahāyāna was awakened; as for the response, the circular hair-tips shone forth.
These six are all called auspicious signs, as the text says:

"Present signs are like the original omens. Omens (*śakuna*) are simply signs; it is human sentiment that distinguishes them, regarding secret intimations as omens and extraordinary occurrences as signs.
What do the marks signify?

The wondrous principle is profound and subtle, making it extremely difficult to explain; human sentiments are often indifferent and unable to show respect. Therefore, one first uses extraordinary marks to startle and transform ordinary sentiments. Once ordinary sentiments are transformed and a sense of reverence and longing arises, one then explains the marks through their significance and explains the signs through their portents.

Briefly clarifying the six auspicious omens that manifest and correspond to the ten subtleties: these were already explained within the "Subtlety of Responsive Manifestation. Now, further explaining the omen of the preaching of the Dharma, it manifests and corresponds to the "Subtlety of Preaching" and the "Subtlety of Wisdom";
the omen of entering meditative concentration manifests and corresponds to the "Subtlety of Practice";
the omen of the falling rain of flowers manifests and corresponds to the "Subtlety of Stages."
The auspicious sign of the earthquake represents the excellence of the environment and the excellence of the vehicle;
the auspicious sign of universal joy represents the excellence of the retinue and the excellence of the benefit;

the auspicious sign of the emission of light represents the excellence of the response and the excellence of the supernormal powers. Therefore, these six types are collectively termed the "Preface of Manifesting Signs."
Regarding "expounding the Mahāyāna sūtras," the *Śīla-sūtra* (Bhadraśīla-sūtra) identifies seven forms of greatness:
first, greatness of the Dharma, which refers to the twelve divisions of the Vaipulya;
second, greatness of mind, which refers to the seeking of bodhi.
3. Greatness of understanding, which refers to understanding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
4. Greatness of purity, which refers to the purification of the mind upon seeing the Path, and so forth;
5. Greatness of adornment, which refers to merit and wisdom.
Sixth, greatness of time, which refers to the practice of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
seventh, greatness of fulfillment, which refers to attaining *bodhi* by adorning oneself with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
The sixth is the greatness of the cause, and the seventh is the greatness of the fruit; with this great cause and great fruit combined, they constitute the Mahāyāna Sūtra.
Now, by selecting the tenfold meaning of the "Marvelous" (daśa-prakāra-vaipulya) and applying it to the sūtra, it should be understood.
Master Sheng said:

"The principle of signless emptiness is the foundation of the Mahāyāna. Because [sentient beings] have been attached to the three vehicles for a long time, they cannot be made to believe in the sudden teaching of the absence of the three; therefore, the teaching of signlessness serves as the introduction to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*."
The Master’s intention seems to be the same.
If that were so, then both the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* should also be considered introductory sections; why then is it only the *Anantamukha-sūtra*?
That Śākya explains:
"In this way, by means of five periods, the subsequent teaching is able to arise.
He asks further:

"If that were so, then the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings) and all other sutras would share a common mode of sequential generation, rather than having a distinct introductory sequence.
Master Ji said:
"Because the principle of emptiness has no form, it is called 'immeasurable. The intent of the introduction is the same as before; the objection is likewise [invalid]."
The Master Yin said:
"Because the perfection of formlessness carries the meaning of attaining Buddhahood, it is called 'immeasurable' (wuliang).
He further stated:

"That sutra does not state that there are three vehicles or that there are no three; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is not what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to, for that which it refers to did not come to the land of Qin."

It is now said that this sutra was received by the bhikṣu Huìbiǎo from Dharmayaśas at Cháozhēn Temple in Nánhǎi Commandery during the third year of the Jiāshí era of the Song dynasty; he subsequently returned to Wǔdāng Mountain, where it was first transmitted to the world in the third year of the Yǒngmíng era.
Since the sutra has already arrived here, how could it be sent back to India?
Guangzhai said:

"The *Anantamukha-sūtra* (Wuliangyi) shows that all myriad virtues converge to enable the attainment of the Buddha-way; the *Lotus Sutra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*) specifically clarifies the non-duality and non-triplicity [of the vehicles], and because its refutation of the three [vehicles] and its establishment of the one are distinct from [the former], it serves as the introduction."
If you say that the myriad virtues all converge upon one point, why do two or three not likewise converge?
If two or three do converge, then the sequence and the rectitude would not differ.
If you say that two and three are to be negated, why not negate the myriad as well?
If one refutes two and refutes three, then there are neither two nor three; since one has already refuted ten thousand, there is then no sequence.

To take passages from the sutras and cite them interchangeably while claiming their intended meaning is different does not establish such difference; if the distinct intention is not revealed, the meaning of the sequence is likewise not established.
Liu Qiu’s commentary states:
“Taking formlessness as the foundation—this single dharma of formlessness contains meanings beyond measure.
If it contains meanings beyond measure, then it possesses form; how can it be called formless?

Upon examining the various masters, each is partial to one particular aspect: if they say that conditioned goodness has the principle of attaining Buddhahood, this is the meaning of the Tripiṭaka Teaching;
if they say that unconditioned goodness has the principle of attaining Buddhahood, this is the meaning of the Shared Teaching;
if they say it encompasses the immeasurable Dharma, this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching.
Furthermore, what is elucidated in other sutras does not, in any way, clarify the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

If the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* enumerates seventeen types [of names], they are all alternative names for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; "The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings" (*Anantārthasūtra*) is simply one of those names.
Now, to state my argument: the Buddha directly spoke these names upon entering this samādhi; therefore, they may serve as the introduction.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, all likewise proclaim the names first; thus, there is no contradiction in their serving as introductions.
Now, in this sutra, Mañjuśrī cites ancient Buddhas who were also named *Ananta-artha* (Infinite Meaning);
furthermore, it says:
"I shall preach the Mahāyāna sūtra named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This is also a proclamation of the title within the introduction, which accords with the intent of the treatise.

Now, according to that sutra, the explanation of "immeasurable meanings" arises from a single dharma; this single dharma is what is called "signlessness. Signlessness and non-sign are termed the "true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa). From this true mark arise immeasurable dharmas, namely: the two dharmas, the three paths, and the four fruits.
Now, to explain this passage: "signless" (animitta) means the absence of the signs of birth and death;
"non-sign" (animitta) means the absence of the sign of nirvāṇa.
Since even nirvāṇa is non-existent, it is called "non-sign and signless," pointing to the Middle Way as the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

The two methods are the sudden and the gradual. "Sudden" refers to all dharmas within the *Avataṃsaka*, while "gradual" refers to all dharmas within the Tripiṭaka, the Vaipulya, and the Prajñāpāramitā.
The three paths are the three vehicles; the four fruits are the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and the buddha. These various dharmas are called "immeasurable.

True reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the locus of meaning (*arthasthāna*); from this single locus of meaning emerge immeasurable dharmas, which serve as the introduction for entering the single locus of meaning through those immeasurable dharmas.

It is like a mathematician who, from a single calculation, brings down all other calculations; by removing all calculations, they return to the single calculation. Because of this bringing down, there is removal, and bringing down serves as the sequence for removal.
From one, he spreads out to all; gathering all back into one, opening [the manifold] becomes the sequence for synthesis—it is just like this.
Explaining it in this manner does not contradict those sutras and treatises, and furthermore accords with this sutra, and so forth.

Moreover, the verses of praise in the *Anantārthika-sūtra* clarify that while the Dharma-body transcends all hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*), its response-manifestation (*nirmāṇakāya*) appears as sixteen feet tall with the radiance of purple-gold.
The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* clarifies that the four pāramitās—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—are the dwelling place [of the Buddha].
Since both the preceding and following passages clarify permanence, how could the intermediate section concerning the lifespan be anything other than permanent?
The opponent raises this objection:
"Since the introduction has already expounded upon permanence, what is there left to be said in the main body?
Now, we shall instead challenge him: Since the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* takes Cunda as its introduction and has already opened the doctrine of permanence, what is there left to be said in the main body?

Furthermore, he cites the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, where the *vajra*-like unconditioned is said to be "incalculable," yet the explicit teaching does not clarify its permanence; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* should be understood in the same way.

Now, let us turn back to challenge this point: if Cunda’s introductory discourse is on permanence, then the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* itself ought to be impermanent; yet now you argue that the introduction concerns permanence—how can the permanence of the sūtra itself not be taken as certain?

Regarding "the teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas," it refers to employing the locus of immeasurable meanings (*ananta-artha-sthāna*) to teach Bodhisattvas; this "locus of meaning" is precisely the principle of the truths (*satya-tattva*).
As stated in the following passage: "Universally causing all multitudes to likewise attain this Way. Furthermore, it says:
"If I encounter sentient beings, I shall teach them all the Buddha-way"—this is precisely that meaning.

Regarding "protected by the Buddha's mindfulness": the *Anantārthasthāna* (The Place of Immeasurable Meanings) is that which the Buddha has personally realized; therefore, it is what the Tathāgata protects with his mindfulness.
The subsequent text states:

"The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna; though he wishes to reveal and instruct, the faculties of sentient beings are dull, so he has long remained silent regarding this essential point, not being intent on expounding it hastily."
Therefore, it is said that he "protects and mindfulness-remembers" [the assembly].

As for the statement, "After the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, he entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings," this indicates that wisdom and concentration mutually accomplish one another: there is no wisdom without dhyāna, so one must first enter concentration; yet there is no dhyāna without wisdom, so he first preached the Dharma.
Wisdom is itself concentration, and concentration is itself wisdom; they enter and emerge from one another without any interval or obstruction.
Those who harbor doubts ask:

"If he had not yet expounded the immeasurable meanings, it would be understandable that he entered this concentration; but now that he has finished preaching this sutra, for what reason does he enter concentration?"
Śāriputra said:
"It can be understood that he first entered this samādhi and afterwards preached this sutra.
That he entered it again after finishing the preaching of this sutra was merely to serve as a prologue for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."

Why is this? If one does not first open [the door], there will be nothing with which to harmonize later; thus, the initial entry into the samādhi of opening serves as the prelude to the samādhi of harmony, and is termed a "portentous sign" (śakuna)—this is precisely that meaning.

If one follows the sequential order, having first entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings, one should then enter the Lotus Samādhi; if this were clearly and manifestly stated, the assembly would understand it immediately. Why, then, wait for Maitreya’s earnest entreaty and Mañjuśrī’s persistent urging? Therefore, we know that the meaning of the introduction becomes even more clarified by its composition.
"Body and mind unmoving" means being in accord with the object of focus.

The fundamental source of the body is as serene as empty space; the nature and principle of the mind are ultimately and eternally tranquil. The body, hands, and feet of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū were still and peacefully unmoving; his mind was constantly calm and serene, never once becoming distracted.

The body is like a vajra, immovable; the mind is like space, free from discrimination. Because the dharmas of the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meanings sustain the body and mind, they do not move.

That which is called "immeasurable" refers to this samādhi, which is tranquil yet constant; its illumination enables the knowledge of the world, for from this single dharma emerge immeasurable dharmas.
If one explains it in terms of the meaning of "introduction" (*nidāna*): the nature of the body-dharma is movement and activity, whereas here it is made non-moving and non-active;
the nature of the mind-dharma is discrimination, whereas here it is made non-discriminative—the meaning of the introduction is thus clarified.
Question:

The auspicious signs described in the original treatise are extraordinary; yet, preaching the Dharma and entering meditative concentration are the Buddha’s constant routines—how can these be considered auspicious signs?
Answer:

Although the preaching of the Dharma had concluded, the assembly did not disperse; they remained solemn and waited for something. Thus we know that when the previous teaching was given, the entire multitude gathered specifically to await what would follow.
This matter is extraordinary and differs from ordinary preaching; how could it not be a portent?

Although he entered the *kaī* (opening) samādhi, his intention was directed toward the *ge* (converging) samādhi; this differs from ordinary entry into samādhi. Why, then, would this not be an auspicious sign?

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī cited that among the six auspicious signs of the ancient Buddhas, all included such an event. If it were not an auspicious sign in the past, how could it serve as proof for the present?
This has been the same from antiquity to the present; how can one disparage it with ordinary sentiments?
Regarding the "four flowers rained down from heaven," the ancients said:
"Small white, large white, small red, and large red."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"The flower of intention (*cittakusuma*) and the great flower of intention, the flower of aspiration (*praṇidhānakusuma*) and the great flower of aspiration.
The *Śāstra* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), fascicle 99, says:
"Among the exquisite celestial flowers, those named *mandārava* are the most sublime.
Furthermore, in the seventy-ninth [chapter], it says:
"In the Buddha-lands of eight hundred bhikṣus, five-colored *mandārava* flowers rain down constantly."

The small and large white [circles] represent the two assemblies of householders; the small and large red [circles] represent the two assemblies of those who have gone forth, signifying that although they have pursued this path since ancient times, they have not yet achieved the fruit.

Now, I maintain that this interpretation is both narrow and incorrect; for even when discussing only the fourfold assembly, it fails to encompass all sixteen assemblies within the Tripiṭaka, let alone the forty-eight assemblies.
Therefore, it is narrow-minded [to say this].
Now, the characteristics of flowers are a close report of their cause; since the fourfold assembly has already been the cause from the past, why wait for the retribution of flowers?
If they were reporting the fruit, the heavens should have rained down actual fruit; why, then, do they rain down flowers?
Therefore, it is said that [the previous causes] were not appropriate.

Now, when we speak of "rain-flowers," this clarifies that the former causes were not the cause of Buddhahood: within the Tripiṭaka, they are the causes of the two vehicles; within the Shared Teaching, they are common causes; and within the Distinct Teaching, they are the causes of bodhisattvas—all of which are not the cause of Buddhahood.
Today’s falling rain signifies that they shall obtain the causes for Buddhahood.

These causes for Buddhahood are the causes of the four wheels: the small white [rain] symbolizes the copper wheel, representing the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the stage of the nature of practice;
the large white [rain] symbolizes the silver wheel, representing the ten practices of the nature of the lineage, which demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The small red represents the wheel of the stage of the lineage of the path and the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*), which is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
the large red represents the wheel of lapis lazuli, the stage of the noble lineage (*āryagotra*) and the ten bhūmis, which is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The four wheels are all identical causes; these causes arise from the center, and thus rain falls from heaven. Because they exist in the state of causality, they are symbolized by flowers.
However, because there is the principle of a cause leading to a result, [the flowers] were scattered upon the Buddha.
As for such cause and effect, who is it that experiences the fruition?
It is none other than the assembly present at this gathering; therefore, it is said, "and the great multitude."

In the subsequent section, Mañjuśrī dispels doubts through the four phrases beginning with "blowing the great dharma-conch," and furthermore, within the formal exposition, there is the sequence of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering. Moreover, in the passage concerning the great chariot, there is the phrase "wandering in the four directions. Since these points are successively linked, they all pertain to the meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*); thus, we know that the flower symbolizes the causal stage.
Question:
The four wheels represent the meaning of distinct stages; how can they explain the stage of perfection?
Answer:
If names are general yet their meanings are complete such that nothing is lost, how much more so when names are distinct yet their meanings are complete—how could they not be employed?
Question:
Regarding the distinct meanings of the worthy and the sages, are there also complete meanings?
Answer:

This has already been explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). If one says that the four flowers fall from the heavens together to symbolize that the fourfold assembly shall collectively achieve the single cause [of Buddhahood], such an interpretation expresses the meaning of the Tripitaka but does not express the universal (pāṭha) meaning.
If one says that the fourfold assembly is equally the cause for Bodhisattvas, this interpretation expresses the universal meaning but does not express the distinct (viśeṣa) meaning.
These are not the causes for Buddhahood, nor do they accord with the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is as previously explained.

Regarding the phrase "the earth in all Buddha-worlds shakes in six ways," the old interpretation—that it refers to shaking the six fixed attachments regarding cause and effect among those of the Three Vehicles—only refutes the six attachments to the Three Vehicles held by the Tripiṭaka masters; it does not yet refute the six attachments to the Three Vehicles held by the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) masters.

In the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*), if one considers the Dharma, the causes and fruits of the three types of persons are identical; yet if one considers the persons themselves, the causes and fruits of these three persons are distinct. Both this identity and this difference are refuted [in the Mahayana], whereas the intent of the "Old School" (the Śrāvaka tradition) does not refute this.
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), since the names of the three vehicles do not exist, there are no six attachments, which were therefore not refuted by the former [teachings].

Now, it is clarified that in the Separate School, the three dharmas are both vertical and horizontal during the causal stage, and the three dharmas are likewise vertical and horizontal at the stage of fruition; this must be refuted.

Now, the sixfold movement of the earth signifies the six successive stages of shattering ignorance within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*). Although ignorance has hitherto remained solid and unassailed, it is now on the verge of being destroyed; thus, the shaking of the earth serves as its manifestation. When ignorance is overturned, it immediately transforms into clarity; therefore, the worlds of all Buddhas tremble in six ways.
The six kinds of manifestations are the sixfold sequence of abiding, proceeding, heading toward, the ground, equality, and excellence.
The *Upāsaka-śuddhacaryā-sūtra* states:

"When a Bodhisattva is born, the earth shakes to demonstrate that this birth is the final one and that there are no further afflictions (*kleśa*). It shakes because the afflictions of all sentient beings who are destined to attain the Way are about to be extinguished."
This is precisely that meaning.

Regarding the interpretation of the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku): it is as when Mañjuśrī resolves doubts by citing ancient Buddhas in response; to secretly grasp this intent is to recognize the fundamental. This does not mean that while other Buddhas previously manifested such auspicious signs, our World-Honored One’s original state was not likewise such signs, but rather that he is not merely a singular instance in the present, and so forth.

The practitioner of contemplation moves the six sense organs; the solidity of the earth-element is like the water-clinging of the six organs. Having not yet entered the path of the Mahāyāna, one moves the ground that is difficult to move, manifesting the roots that are both pure and impure.
Regarding "the east surges up while the west sinks down": the east is green and presides over the liver, and the liver presides over the eyes;

the west is white and presides over the lungs, and the lungs preside over the nose. This signifies that as the merit of the eye-faculty arises, the afflictions of the nose-faculty are extinguished; and as the merit of the nose-faculty arises, the afflictions within the eyes are extinguished. The surging and sinking in the other directions likewise signify the arising and ceasing of the remaining faculties in the same manner.
The six types of movement are: shaking, rising, surging, quaking, roaring, and awakening. Within each of these, there are further three:
namely, shaking, universal shaking, and equal universal shaking.

Movement in one direction is called "movement"; movement throughout the four continents is called "universal movement"; and movement throughout the great trichiliocosm is called "equal universal movement.
The same applies to the other five types of movement; together they constitute eighteen kinds of movement, which symbolize the purification of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), and so forth.

Next, to clarify the auspicious omen of the great assembly’s joyful hearts: when the multitude saw the falling rain of flowers and the shaking of the earth, they knew that the nectar was about to descend; their inner joy overflowed, signifying that their great capacity for awakening was about to be activated, thereby eliciting a sublime response from the Buddha.
Question:
Joy and anger are the common emotions of human beings; how can they constitute an auspicious omen?
Answer:
Celestial flowers gladden the eyes, and the earth’s trembling shakes the heart. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"When it moves, it can cause the hearts of sentient beings to move.

The flowers and the earth are external auspicious signs, while the joy in the heart is an internal auspicious sign.
